canonical_topic: Base load, peak load, and safety-margin generation
definition: Base load is the minimum level of demand a region must meet at all times, typically supplied by baseload generation units. Peak load is the expected maximum level of demand, which requires nearly all of a region's generation units to run. Many regions also hold extra generation capacity as a safety margin that may rarely or never run under normal conditions.
core_idea: A region's demand profile spans a floor (base load) and a ceiling (peak load), and grid operators keep reserve capacity beyond the peak as insurance against unexpected contingencies.
key_points: Base load = minimum demand that must always be met; served by baseload generation units.
Peak load = expected maximum demand; meeting it requires nearly all generation units in the region to operate.
Safety-margin units are extra generation held in reserve, which may never be dispatched under normal conditions.
These three concepts frame what a spatial load forecast is trying to estimate: expected demand, maximum demand, and the buffer needed above it.
relationships: Both are quantities a spatial load forecast must estimate for capacity planning
trading_implications: Peak load periods are when nearly all generation is engaged, which is relevant context for understanding price spikes.
